title: I’m a retired auto dealer who built a stock-picking system. Here are my 5 Month results.
author: Prestigious_Bridge50
selftext:
I spent 35 years in the auto business. Since retiring, I’ve been building an AI stock research system. I now have about five and a half months of testing, starting June 1.

I’d like people who have built or evaluated something similar to pick it apart. I’m keeping the exact methods private, but I can show the results, how many stocks were involved, and where things haven’t gone as well. I’ll call the signals Composite, Signal 1, and Signal 2, and use letters for the portfolios.

# What the replay showed

I tested eight portfolio versions over June 1 through November 11, 2026. The replay summary reports returns ranging from **+9.47% to +17.78%**, with an average of **+15.15%**. SPY rose **0.59%** from the June 1 open to the November 11 close, excluding dividends.

These were broad portfolios. Depending on the version, they held an average of about **40 to 206 stocks at a time**. Across all eight, the replay summary records **2,963 positions opened across 546 different stocks**. That includes repeat purchases and stocks appearing in more than one portfolio.

Here’s the win/loss breakdown at the November 11 cutoff:

* **1,926 positions had closed:** 1,189 were profitable, and 737 lost money or finished flat. That’s a **61.7% closed-position win rate**.
* **1,037 positions were still open:** 686 showed gains, and 351 showed losses or were flat.

Combined, that’s **1,875 positive positions and 1,088 losing or flat**, or **63.3% positive including the open positions**. The open positions covered 297 distinct stocks across the eight portfolios.

There are a few problems in that history I can’t ignore. The portfolio rules were finalized after some of the summer data was already available. Financial inputs before July 10 had a known bug. And June 1 has a timing problem: the signals came out after the market opened, while the replay could buy at that morning’s opening price. I still need to measure what correcting that does to the results.

The replay compounds an average of daily position returns. It isn’t a fixed funded account, and the cost assumptions differ between versions.

# The signals themselves

Separately, I checked the signals against later stock returns.

That study covers signals dated **June 1 through October 19**, using the stored forward-return measure of roughly one month relative to SPY. It includes **21 weekly checks, 26,523 stock-week observations and 1,276 distinct stocks**.

|Signal|Average weekly IC|IC after sector and factor controls|Positive raw-IC weeks|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Composite|0.1440|0.1211|21 of 21|
|Signal 1|0.1335|0.1056|21 of 21|
|Signal 2|0.1739|0.1128|20 of 21|

What interests me is how much of the relationship remains after the controls. Composite’s raw IC was positive in all 21 weekly checks.

Still, the return windows overlap, and many of the same companies appear each week. Twenty-one weekly readings don’t give me 21 independent tests. The earlier financial-input problem applies here too.

# The forward paper record

The eight paper portfolios launched at different times. Their earliest common window is **October 15 through November 18**, covering **25 trading sessions**.

Over that period, recorded returns range from **+0.27% to +4.66%**. The portfolios currently hold between **45 and 219 stocks each**, with **288 distinct stocks** across the eight.

Portfolio A leads that window at **+4.66%**, holding 219 stocks. It closed 46 positions during the period, and 36 were profitable (**78.3%)**. Those are full entry-to-exit results for the positions closed during the window; some were bought earlier.

But take that same portfolio back to its September 3 start and its recorded return is **−0.44%**, with **54 winners and 53 losses among its completed positions**. That’s a **50.5% win rate** over the longer record.

Portfolio A includes 0.10% modeled execution cost per side. Three holdings still use older prices, so the latest result is provisional. The forward books measure daily P&L relative to deployed capital, which differs from the historical replay calculation.

There are also three newer experimental paper books whose first purchases were October 19. They’re down **1.64% to 7.92%** through November 18, and there are gaps in their recorded daily decisions.

# Two honest questions

Looking at the gap between the June–November replays and the noisier forward paper results, what’s the biggest red flag I might be explaining away because I want this to work?

And if the forward results do hold up, where would you see something like this fitting? I won’t put my name on it or charge anyone for it without six to twelve months of forward testing that stands up, with the signals locked before each market open. If it clears that bar, would you keep it for trading your own money, build research software for advisers or institutions, or take it in another direction?

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
the biggest red flag to me is the IC itself. a weekly IC around 0.14 for roughly one-month returns, positive in every check, is much stronger than what usually survives in cross-sectional stock signals. when a signal looks that clean, the first suspect is lookahead: fundamentals stamped with the period date instead of the date they were actually published, the input bug before july 10, or the open-price entry you mentioned. I'd rebuild the study using only data with its real release timestamp and see how much of the 0.14 is left.  
two smaller things: compare the broad portfolios with an equal-weight basket of the same universe, not SPY, since 40–200 names behave very differently from a cap-weighted index. and I'd treat portfolio A from september 3 as the honest number so far, since that's the one picked before seeing the outcome.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The biggest red flag is one you already named. The rules were set after some of the summer data was visible, so the replay isn't a clean test, and the gap between the replay and the forward results is what that usually looks like. Portfolio A going from a good recent window to about flat since its September start also shows how much the window matters. I'd treat only the forward record as real evidence, and I'd compare it with an equal-weight basket of the same stocks, since beating SPY alone can come from the stock universe, not the signals. If you want a tool for the history side, Cymetica's Backtest Labs holds out the last part of the data.
